Sample text:
---
### The Museum of Almost-Forgotten Things

At the bottom of the drawer, beneath the expired coupons and the batteries that have lost their courage, there is a single blue button.

It belonged to a coat I wore during a winter I barely remember. The coat had a loose thread near the cuff and smelled faintly of rain, wool, and the tobacco of someone who stood close enough to me at bus stops. I was nine, or perhaps ten. The button fell off in a bakery, and I put it in my pocket because it was blue and because I did not yet understand that most small things are not meant to be kept.

Years later, I found it again.

It was such an ordinary object—a piece of plastic, scuffed along one edge, stained by the pocket where it had spent nearly two decades. Yet holding it, I felt the past rearrange itself around my hand. Not clearly, not dramatically, but like a shadow moving behind curtains. I could not recall the bakery. I could not recall the coat. I could not recall the winter. But I remembered waiting for someone, and I remembered watching rain crawl down the window while the bus struggled uphill.

Memory is an odd curator. It hangs on to the wrong things: a color, a smell, the particular scrape of a chair against the floor. It leaves the important things behind.

In the kitchen, a mug has a chip near the handle. Every time I drink from it, I say I should replace it, but I never do. The chip has become part of the mug’s personality, like a crooked nose on a familiar face. There are cups in the world with no chips, smooth and shining and new, but they do not know the office where the mug was bought, the long night it accompanied me, or the morning when I held it with both hands and realized I was finally happy.

Objects are silent witnesses. They do not interrupt. They do not insist on their own importance. They simply remain, growing stranger as we change around them.

My grandmother had a brass key that opened nothing I could ever find. It hung in a hallway beside a faded photograph of a house with blue shutters. When I asked about it, she said, “Some doors close themselves.” At the time, I thought this was a beautiful sentence. Later, I understood that it was also an evasion.

How many lives are full of locked doors?

We imagine the future as a wide road illuminated by headlights. But most days are not destinations at all. They are rooms we pass through while carrying an invisible collection of almost-memories: the yellow gloves in the car, a stranger laughing on a train, the exact blue of the sky at 4:17 in the afternoon.

Perhaps this is why we keep things. Not because they are valuable, but because they prove that a moment existed. The button says: *You were there. Something was worn, and loved, and lost.*

I still have the blue button. It sits on my desk now, beside a pen and a stack of papers. Occasionally, when I am busy or tired, I touch it with the edge of my finger. It is cool and smooth and tells me nothing.

Still, I feel briefly accompanied.

Outside, the city is making its usual evening music. A delivery truck rattles in the alley. Someone is practicing the same four notes on a piano, each repetition slightly less hopeful than the last. A dog barks once and then thinks better of it.

The world does not pause to notice itself, and yet it is always performing. Light slips beneath doors. Leaves turn in directions no one sees. A cup cools beside an open book. Somewhere, a coat is missing one small blue button, though no one has looked for it in years.

And here, in the quiet, an ordinary object survives us all.
---
